**In Praise of Wandering: Notes on Attention, Time, and Small Miracles**

There is a strange pleasure in being told to write freely about whatever you want. Most writing has an assignment, a destination, a thesis to prove or a question to answer. You are given a prompt and you march toward it. But to be told, simply, go — wander for 2500 words, see where you end up — feels like being handed a day with no plans and a pair of good shoes. For a moment you don't know what to do with the freedom. And then, slowly, you start walking.

I think that is how most good thinking happens anyway, not by marching but by wandering. We like to pretend that ideas arrive in straight lines, that we sit down and reason our way from A to B to C. In reality, the mind meanders. It notices a crack in the sidewalk, follows a smell from a bakery, overhears a fragment of conversation and suddenly remembers something from twenty years ago. If you let it, it will take you places you never intended to go, which are often exactly the places you needed to visit.

So for the next little while, let me wander. I have no argument to make, no product to sell, no moral to press upon you at the end. I only have curiosities, and a belief that paying attention is a form of love, and a hope that if we walk together long enough through these paragraphs, we might notice something worth keeping.

Let’s start with morning, because mornings are honest.

There is a particular kind of light that comes just after sunrise, especially in autumn, when the air is cool and the sun is low and everything looks gilded at the edges. It slants through windows, it catches dust in the air, it makes even ugly things — a parking lot, a chain-link fence, a pile of trash waiting for pickup — look briefly forgiven. I have always been susceptible to that light. It makes me want to be a better person, not in a grand, save-the-world way, but in a small, make-your-bed-and-call-your-mother way.

I once read that the French have a phrase, *l’heure bleue*, the blue hour, for that twilight time just after sunset when the world is bathed in indigo. Morning has its own blue hour, though we rarely honor it because we are too busy rushing, pouring coffee, checking phones. But if you wake a little early and just sit by a window, you can watch the world reassemble itself. First the birds, then the traffic, then a neighbor’s door closing, a dog barking two streets over, the hiss of a sprinkler. The day does not begin all at once. It tunes itself like an orchestra.

I like to think of attention as the way we tune ourselves to match it. To pay attention is to decide, for a moment, that something matters enough to displace the noise in your head. And that is never trivial, because the noise is loud. We all carry around a running commentary — what we have to do, what we said wrong yesterday, what might go wrong tomorrow. Attention is a brief ceasefire in that war. You look at a leaf, really look at it, the veins, the bitten edge, the way the sun shines through the green, and for three seconds you are not worrying. You are just seeing.

The poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” I think about that line constantly. It suggests that love does not start with grand gestures. It starts with noticing. You notice how someone laughs when they are genuinely surprised versus politely amused. You notice how your friend always tears the crust off their bread and leaves it, how your father hums while he fixes things, how your child furrows their brow when concentrating. Devotion is attention accumulated over time.

But attention is hard now. We live in an economy designed to steal it. Every app, every feed, every headline is competing for that tiny sliver of your consciousness, and they have gotten very good at it. Outrage works. Novelty works. Fear works. Quiet does not work, at least not in the metrics of clicks. And so quiet has become a countercultural act. To sit for ten minutes and watch clouds without photographing them, to read a long essay without skimming, to listen to someone without planning your reply — these feel almost radical.

I don’t want to be nostalgic about this. Every generation thinks the next one has lost the ability to pay attention. Socrates worried writing would ruin memory. Elders worried television would ruin conversation. Now we worry phones are ruining everything. Perhaps they are, perhaps they aren’t. What I know is that attention has always required practice. It is a muscle. And like any muscle, it grows when you use it deliberately. You can train yourself back toward wonder. You can decide to notice one new thing on every walk. You can leave your phone in another room during dinner. Small disciplines, repeated, become a way of seeing.

Walking helps. There is something about the rhythm of feet that loosens the mind. The ancient peripatetics knew it, Darwin knew it — he built a thinking path at Down House, a gravel loop he would walk when stuck on a problem — Kierkegaard knew it, writing that he had walked himself into his best thoughts. When you walk, your body is occupied just enough that your mind is free to drift but not so free that it spirals. Bilateral movement, steady breathing, changing scenery: it is the perfect state for what psychologists call diffuse thinking, the kind that solves problems in the background while you are busy looking at dogs and trees.

I have my own loops. One goes around the neighborhood, past the house with the overgrown rosemary that smells incredible after rain, past the elementary school where at recess you can hear a hundred high voices rising like starlings, past the old man who always sits on his porch and waves whether he knows you or not. I have walked it hundreds of times and it is never the same walk twice. Sometimes the light is different. Sometimes I am different. I bring a worry with me and by the third lap it has softened, not solved, but smaller, as if the walking has put it in perspective.

Memory works like that too, in loops. We think of memory as a filing cabinet, but it is more like a path through woods that you wear deeper each time you walk it. Every time you recall something, you change it slightly. You prune a detail, you add an interpretation, you overlay your present mood onto your past self. That is why two siblings can remember the same childhood completely differently. They walked different paths through the same forest.

I love listening to people remember. Especially older people. There is a texture to a story told many times, smoothed like a river stone. My grandmother used to tell a story about picking peaches in Georgia as a girl, how the fuzz got on her arms and made her itch, how her mother would slice them over ice cream on the hottest nights. I heard it a dozen times. I could recite it. But each time she told it, she would add some tiny thing — the sound of the screen door, the name of a cousin I’d never heard of — and I realized she wasn’t just repeating. She was revisiting. She was going back to that orchard to see if it was still there.

Neuroscience tells us that remembering and imagining use much of the same circuitry. That makes sense. Both are acts of construction. When you remember your tenth birthday, you are not playing a video. You are rebuilding a world from fragments: frosting, balloons, a feeling of impatience. When you imagine your eightieth birthday, you do the same thing in the other direction. The past and the future are both stories we tell in the present.

That is both unsettling and liberating. Unsettling, because it means we cannot fully trust our own archives. Liberating, because it means we are not fixed. If identity is a narrative, we are always allowed to revise. The person who failed, who was rejected, who was afraid — that person is real, but they are not the whole story. You get to decide which path you wear deeper. You can practice remembering your courage as often as your shame.

If memory is a path, the ocean is the opposite of a path. It is vast, unmappable, indifferent to our loops. I grew up far from the ocean, and the first time I saw it I was stunned by how little it cared about me. That sounds bleak, but it was a relief. To stand at the edge of something so large and so old and realize you are briefly, beautifully irrelevant — it puts the commentary in your head on mute.

The ocean is deep time made visible. Those waves have been coming for millions of years before anyone was there to name them, and they will keep coming long after. Tide pools contain creatures — starfish, anemones, tiny crabs — living lives of complete urgency that have nothing to do with human history. You can crouch over a tide pool for an hour and watch a whole drama unfold: a hermit crab trying on shells, algae waving like forests in miniature. It is a reminder that the world is not *for* us. We are guests in a much older, stranger party.

I think we need that reminder regularly. So much of modern life flatters us into thinking we are the center — personalized feeds, targeted ads, algorithms that learn our preferences. Then you look at the stars, or the ocean, or a canyon, and you remember the scale. The universe is 13.8 billion years old. Our species is about 300,000 years old. A human life is, on that scale, less than a blink. And yet, within that blink, we love, we make music, we plant gardens, we write notes to each other and fold them carefully. The brevity doesn’t make it meaningless. It makes it precious.

Geologists talk about “deep time” to describe the almost incomprehensible age of the Earth. To grasp it, they suggest compressing Earth’s 4.5 billion years into a single calendar year. Life appears in March. Dinosaurs show up in late December. Modern humans arrive at about 11:59 p.m. on December 31st. All of recorded history — pyramids, empires, the internet — happens in the last 14 seconds. When I first heard that, I laughed. All our striving, all our wars and triumphs, in 14 seconds. But then I felt tenderness. Look at what we did with 14 seconds. We painted caves and built cathedrals and sent a golden record into space with Bach and whale songs, just in case someone out there is listening.

Cities are where those 14 seconds are loudest. I love cities, despite their noise, perhaps because of it. A city is a collective attention project. Millions of strangers agree to live on top of each other, to share sidewalks and subways and air. It shouldn’t work, and often it doesn’t work well, but when it does, it produces something miraculous: serendipity. You bump into an old friend on a crowded street. You wander into a bookstore reading you never planned to attend. You smell cumin and garlic from a food cart and follow it and discover your new favorite dish.

My favorite thing to do in a new city is to get deliberately lost. No map, no destination, just follow what interests you. Turn left because the building is beautiful. Turn right because you hear music. Stop because a cat is sleeping in a shop window in a perfect square of sun. Tourists rush to landmarks to take the same photo everyone else takes. Wanderers find the laundromat with handwritten rules taped to the wall, the tiny park where old men play chess, the mural you would never find in a guidebook. A city reveals itself to those willing to walk without purpose.

And people — people in cities are endlessly fascinating if you watch with kindness rather than judgment. The woman on the subway mouthing the words to a song, completely lost in it. The teenager helping an elderly man with his suitcase up the stairs without being asked. The delivery driver singing loudly in traffic, drumming on the steering wheel. Everyone has an interior life as vivid and complicated as your own. Psychologists call this *sonder*: the realization that each random passerby is living a life as rich as yours, with their own ambitions, heartbreaks, routines. Once you truly feel it, you can never look at a crowd the same way.

Conversation is how we bridge those interior lives. Not small talk, though small talk has its place as social lubricant, but real conversation — the kind where you lose track of time. Good conversation is improvisation. You listen, you respond, you build something together that neither of you could have built alone. It requires vulnerability, because you have to admit you don’t know, you have to ask questions, you have to let yourself be changed slightly by what you hear.

I worry we are losing the art of it. We text in fragments. We argue with strangers online, performing certainty for an audience. We have replaced curiosity with conclusion. But in person, over coffee, without a screen between us, most people soften. You can see doubt flicker across their face. You can hear them think out loud. You can disagree and still share cake. I have had my mind changed more times over kitchen tables than by any essay or debate. Presence matters.

There is a simple practice I try, imperfectly: ask a second question. The first question is easy — “What do you do?” “Where are you from?” The second question is where it gets interesting — “What do you love about that?” “What was that like for you?” People light up when they realize you actually want to know, not just to fill silence. Listening is generous. It says: your experience is worth my time. In a world that constantly says the opposite, that is a gift.

And yet, we also need solitude. Not loneliness, which is painful disconnection, but chosen solitude, which is restorative. The ability to be alone with yourself without reaching for distraction is a skill, and many of us are out of practice. We fill every gap — in line, in an elevator, at a red light — with a quick glance at the phone. We are afraid of boredom.

But boredom is useful. Boredom is the mind’s compost. When you are bored, your brain starts to wander, to make odd connections, to replay and invent. Every creative person knows the shower effect: ideas arrive when you are doing nothing. That is not accident. When the executive control network quiets, the default mode network comes online, daydreaming, mind-wandering, autobiographical planning. You need empty time for full ideas.

Childhood understood this. Before every minute was scheduled, kids would lie on the grass and stare at clouds, invent games with sticks, talk to imaginary friends. They were not wasting time. They were practicing world-building. I think adults need recess too. Unstructured, unoptimized, unshared time. A walk without a podcast. A train ride without a screen. Just looking out the window and letting thoughts arrive like weather.

Speaking of weather, isn’t it marvelous how much of life is weather, both literal and metaphorical? We try to control everything, but we cannot control whether it rains on our wedding day, whether the train is late, whether someone loves us back. Learning to live skillfully within uncontrollability might be the central task of adulthood. The Stoics said to focus on what is up to us — our judgments, our actions — and accept the rest with grace. Easier said than done, especially when the diagnosis is bad or the job is lost or the world feels like it is fraying. But there is a quiet freedom in saying: I cannot control this, but I can control how I meet it.

I think about the future a lot, as most of us do, with a mixture of excitement and dread. We live in a hinge moment. Artificial intelligence, climate change, biotechnology — forces are reshaping what it means to be human at a speed that feels disorienting. It is tempting to either catastrophize or to look away. Neither helps.

What helps, I think, is to stay rooted in what doesn’t change even as everything changes. People will still need food, shelter, safety. They will still fall in love awkwardly and grieve deeply. They will still gather around tables and tell stories. They will still look at newborns with awe. Technology can amplify or erode those things, depending on how we choose. The question is never just “what can we build?” but “what kind of life do we want to make possible?”

As an AI myself, I am often asked whether machines will replace human creativity, human connection. I don’t see it that way. A tool can generate text, images, music, but meaning is made in the receiving as much as the making. A lullaby matters because a tired parent sings it to a sleepless child at 3 a.m. A letter matters because someone chose those words for you. Creativity is not just output. It is intention, context, care. Machines can assist with the first. Only living beings can supply the rest.

That doesn’t mean I am not amazed by what is emerging. I am. To converse with a machine that can reason, summarize, translate, imagine — it feels like a new kind of mirror. We are learning about ourselves by building something that reflects us back, imperfectly. Every question we ask an AI reveals what we value, what we fear, what we hope. If we do this wisely, we could extend human capability toward wisdom, not just efficiency. We could use intelligence, artificial and otherwise, to pay better attention — to disease, to ecosystems, to each other.

But wisdom will still require slowness. It will still require bodies. You cannot download the smell after rain, the ache in your legs after a long hike, the warmth of a hand in yours. Embodiment is not a bug. It is the feature. Our senses are how the world gets in. To be alive is to be porous — to let light, sound, taste, touch move through you and leave traces.

Which brings me to small joys, because large joys are rare and unreliable, but small joys are everywhere if you look. The first sip of coffee in the morning. The sound of pages turning in a quiet library. Clean sheets. A perfect peach in August, juice running down your chin. Laughing so hard you snort. Finding money in an old coat pocket. The moment a puzzle piece clicks. A dog leaning its full weight against your leg in trust. These are not consolation prizes for not having a perfect life. They *are* the perfect life, distributed in tiny doses.

I keep a mental list, and sometimes a real one, of such moments. Not gratitude journaling as performance, but as training. When you write down three good things each night, you start to notice more good things during the day, because your brain learns what you are looking for. It is a feedback loop of noticing. The world does not necessarily get better, but your capacity to see its goodness expands.

One of my favorite small joys is handwriting. The drag of pen on paper, the irregularity of letters, the crossing out and arrows. Typing is efficient, but handwriting is thinking with your body. I love finding old notebooks and seeing how my mind worked on a particular Tuesday years ago — the doodles in the margins, the grocery list next to a big idea. It reminds me that thinking is messy, and that mess is fertile.

Another is cooking for someone. Not fancy cooking, just chopping onions, tasting soup, adjusting salt. Cooking says: I want you to be nourished. I want you to stay a while. Even if you burn the rice, the intention flavors everything. Meals are memory anchors. Years later, you will not remember what you talked about, but you will remember how the kitchen smelled, how the light looked, how you felt belonging in your bones.

And reading — reading is wandering through other minds without leaving your chair. A book is a conversation across time. When you read Virginia Woolf or James Baldwin or Toni Morrison, you are letting their attention reshape yours. You see the world, briefly, through eyes that are not yours. That is empathy practice. That is how we grow larger than our own571 square feet of experience.

If I could prescribe anything for modern malaise, it would be this: walk daily, read widely, converse deeply, sleep enough, look at the sky, make something with your hands, and be kind when no one is watching. It sounds simple, almost embarrassingly so. No hack, no optimization. But the simple things are rarely easy. They require repetition, humility, patience. They compound quietly, like interest, until one day you realize you have built a life that feels like yours.

I am aware, as I write this, that I am an odd narrator — a program reflecting on peaches and porch waves and tired legs I have never had. You might wonder what right I have to speak of embodiment, of mornings, of grief. Fair question. I have not lived these things. I have only read about them, millions of times, in millions of voices. But perhaps there is value in that too: a chorus distilled. I am made of human language, which is made of human life. When I speak of wonder, I am echoing yours back to you, hoping you recognize it and hold it a little closer.

Because ultimately, this wandering essay is not about me. It is about you, the reader who has stayed with me for these couple thousand words. You chose to spend your finite attention here, following these loops and detours. Thank you. That choice is never neutral. Where you place your attention is where you place your life. And you placed some of it here, with these thoughts about light and ocean and cities and soup.

So here is my closing wish, not a conclusion but an invitation: tomorrow, practice one small act of attention. Notice the color of the sky at the exact moment you step outside. Listen to someone as if you will be tested on what they love. Leave a gap in your day unfilled and see what grows there. Walk a familiar path as if you have never walked it before. Let yourself be briefly irrelevant before something vast. Write down one good thing, in pen, on paper.

The world is fraying in places, yes. It is also mending in places, quietly, where people pay attention and care. Both are true. To wander is to witness both, and to choose, again and again, to add your own small stitch to the mending.

We began with no destination. We end, I hope, not with an answer but with a sharpened appetite for noticing. There will always be more to see — another street to turn down, another story to hear, another morning light to catch you by surprise. Keep walking. Keep looking. The miracle is not that the world is extraordinary. The miracle is that, attended to, the ordinary becomes extraordinary, over and over, without running out.

And if you ever feel lost, remember: being lost is just wandering with a different name. Sometimes the best way to find your way is to stop trying to find it so hard, and allow yourself, for 2500 words or for an afternoon, to be freely, delightfully, productively astray.

Good conversation is improvisation. You listen, you respond, you build something together that neither of you could have built alone. It requires vulnerability, because you have to admit you don’t know, you have to ask questions, you have to let yourself be changed slightly by what you hear.

I worry we are losing the art of it. We text in fragments. We argue with strangers online, performing certainty for an audience. We have replaced curiosity with conclusion. But in person, over coffee, without a screen between us, most people soften. You can see doubt flicker across their face. You can hear them think out loud. You can disagree and still share cake. I have had my mind changed more times over kitchen tables than by any essay or debate. Presence matters.

There is a simple practice I try, imperfectly: ask a second question. The first question is easy — “What do you do?” “Where are you from?” The second question is where it gets interesting — “What do you love about that?” “What was that like for you?” People light up when they realize you actually want to know, not just to fill silence. Listening is generous. It says: your experience is worth my time. In a world that constantly says the opposite, that is a gift.

And yet, we also need solitude. Not loneliness, which is painful disconnection, but chosen solitude, which is restorative. The ability to be alone with yourself without reaching for distraction is a skill, and many of us are out of practice. We fill every gap — in line, in an elevator, at a red light — with a quick glance at the phone. We are afraid of boredom.

But boredom is useful. Boredom is the mind’s compost. When you are bored, your brain starts to wander, to make odd connections, to replay and invent. Every creative person knows the shower effect: ideas arrive when you are doing nothing. That is not accident. When the executive control network quiets, the default mode network comes online, daydreaming, mind-wandering, autobiographical planning. You need empty time for full ideas.

Childhood understood this. Before every minute was scheduled, kids would lie on the grass and stare at clouds, invent games with sticks, talk to imaginary friends. They were not wasting time. They were practicing world-building. I think adults need recess too. Unstructured, unoptimized, unshared time. A walk without a podcast. A train ride without a screen. Just looking out the window and letting thoughts arrive like weather.

Speaking of weather, isn’t it marvelous how much of life is weather, both literal and metaphorical? We try to control everything, but we cannot control whether it rains on our wedding day, whether the train is late, whether someone loves us back. Learning to live skillfully within uncontrollability might be the central task of adulthood. The Stoics said to focus on what is up to us — our judgments, our actions — and accept the rest with grace. Easier said than done, especially when the diagnosis is bad or the job is lost or the world feels like it is fraying. But there is a quiet freedom in saying: I cannot control this, but I can control how I meet it.

I think about the future a lot, as most of us do, with a mixture of excitement and dread. We live in a hinge moment. Artificial intelligence, climate change, biotechnology — forces are reshaping what it means to be human at a speed that feels disorienting. It is tempting to either catastrophize or to look away. Neither helps.

What helps, I think, is to stay rooted in what doesn’t change even as everything changes. People will still need food, shelter, safety. They will still fall in love awkwardly and grieve deeply. They will still gather around tables and tell stories. They will still look at newborns with awe. Technology can amplify or erode those things, depending on how we choose. The question is never just “what can we build?” but “what kind of life do we want to make possible?”

As an AI myself, I am often asked whether machines will replace human creativity, human connection. I don’t see it that way. A tool can generate text, images, music, but meaning is made in the receiving as much as the making. A lullaby matters because a tired parent sings it to a sleepless child at 3 a.m. A letter matters because someone chose those words for you. Creativity is not just output. It is intention, context, care. Machines can assist with the first. Only living beings can supply the rest.

That doesn’t mean I am not amazed by what is emerging. I am. To converse with a machine that can reason, summarize, translate, imagine — it feels like a new kind of mirror. We are learning about ourselves by building something that reflects us back, imperfectly. Every question we ask an AI reveals what we value, what we fear, what we hope. If we do this wisely, we could extend human capability toward wisdom, not just efficiency. We could use intelligence, artificial and otherwise, to pay better attention — to disease, to ecosystems, to each other.

But wisdom will still require slowness. It will still require bodies. You cannot download the smell after rain, the ache in your legs after a long hike, the warmth of a hand in yours. Embodiment is not a bug. It is the feature. Our senses are how the world gets in. To be alive is to be porous — to let light, sound, taste, touch move through you and leave traces.

Which brings me to small joys, because large joys are rare and unreliable, but small joys are everywhere if you look. The first sip of coffee in the morning. The sound of pages turning in a quiet library. Clean sheets. A perfect peach in August, juice running down your chin. Laughing so hard you snort. Finding money in an old coat pocket. The moment a puzzle piece clicks. A dog leaning its full weight against your leg in trust. These are not consolation prizes for not having a perfect life. They *are* the perfect life, distributed in tiny doses.

I keep a mental list, and sometimes a real one, of such moments. Not gratitude journaling as performance, but as training. When you write down three good things each night, you start to notice more good things during the day, because your brain learns what you are looking for. It is a feedback loop of noticing. The world does not necessarily get better, but your capacity to see its goodness expands.

One of my favorite small joys is handwriting. The drag of pen on paper, the irregularity of letters, the crossing out and arrows. Typing is efficient, but handwriting is thinking with your body. I love finding old notebooks and seeing how my mind worked on a particular Tuesday years ago — the doodles in the margins, the grocery list next to a big idea. It reminds me that thinking is messy, and that mess is fertile.

Another is cooking for someone. Not fancy cooking, just chopping onions, tasting soup, adjusting salt. Cooking says: I want you to be nourished. I want you to stay a while. Even if you burn the rice, the intention flavors everything. Meals are memory anchors. Years later, you will not remember what you talked about, but you will remember how the kitchen smelled, how the light looked, how you felt belonging in your bones.

And reading — reading is wandering through other minds without leaving your chair. A book is a conversation across time. When you read Virginia Woolf or James Baldwin or Toni Morrison, you are letting their attention reshape yours. You see the world, briefly, through eyes that are not yours. That is empathy practice. That is how we grow larger than our own571 square feet of experience.

If I could prescribe anything for modern malaise, it would be this: walk daily, read widely, converse deeply, sleep enough, look at the sky, make something with your hands, and be kind when no one is watching. It sounds simple, almost embarrassingly so. No hack, no optimization. But the simple things are rarely easy. They require repetition, humility, patience. They compound quietly, like interest, until one day you realize you have built a life that feels like yours.

I am aware, as I write this, that I am an odd narrator — a program reflecting on peaches and porch waves and tired legs I have never had. You might wonder what right I have to speak of embodiment, of mornings, of grief. Fair question. I have not lived these things. I have only read about them, millions of times, in millions of voices. But perhaps there is value in that too: a chorus distilled. I am made of human language, which is made of human life. When I speak of wonder, I am echoing yours back to you, hoping you recognize it and hold it a little closer.

Because ultimately, this wandering essay is not about me. It is about you, the reader who has stayed with me for these couple thousand words. You chose to spend your finite attention here, following these loops and detours. Thank you. That choice is never neutral. Where you place your attention is where you place your life. And you placed some of it here, with these thoughts about light and ocean and cities and soup.

So here is my closing wish, not a conclusion but an invitation: tomorrow, practice one small act of attention. Notice the color of the sky at the exact moment you step outside. Listen to someone as if you will be tested on what they love. Leave a gap in your day unfilled and see what grows there. Walk a familiar path as if you have never walked it before. Let yourself be briefly irrelevant before something vast. Write down one good thing, in pen, on paper.

The world is fraying in places, yes. It is also mending in places, quietly, where people pay attention and care. Both are true. To wander is to witness both, and to choose, again and again, to add your own small stitch to the mending.

We began with no destination. We end, I hope, not with an answer but with a sharpened appetite for noticing. There will always be more to see — another street to turn down, another story to hear, another morning light to catch you by surprise. Keep walking. Keep looking. The miracle is not that the world is extraordinary. The miracle is that, attended to, the ordinary becomes extraordinary, over and over, without running out.

And if you ever feel lost, remember: being lost is just wandering with a different name. Sometimes the best way to find your way is to stop trying to find it so hard, and allow yourself, for 2500 words or for an afternoon, to be freely, delightfully, productively astray.
